text.tspan: Section 3.1: Measures of Center
Figure 3.4
: The addition of the extremely low observations drags the mean away from the center.
Example 2 shows that the mean is sensitive to extreme observations, meaning that observations that are
far from the rest will pull the mean in their direction. That makes the mean an unreliable measurement
in the cases where there are extremely high or extremely low data values. In the example you can see
that the scores of 0 and 10 dragged the mean so much lower that it failed to be a good measure of a
typical exam score.
Important Point!
The
mean
is
sensitive
to extreme observations. If there are extreme values among the data, the
mean will be pulled in their direction. For this reason, the mean is not a good measure of center
when there are extreme values present in the data.
This happens because the value of
every observation
is included in the calculation of the arithmetic
mean. Every data value carries weight in the computation, so every data value has influence over the
value of the mean. As a result, even one or two extreme values can ruin the mean’s ability to measure
the center of the data. In the cases where we have extreme values, we need another way to look at what
it means to be typical. That’s where the median comes into play.
The Median
A second way to identify a typical value is to arrange the data in order, from smallest to largest, then find
the value or values that are right in the middle of the list. This is called finding the
median
. Like the
mean, the formulas can be confusing, but the idea is straight-forward.
Extremely low scores
drag the mean lower.
